newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia health, biotech companies get own index.
newsitem.headline: Australia health, biotech companies get own index.

text.p: Australia's health and biotechnology companies are set to emerge from the anonymity of the miscellaneous indices next month, when they get their own index on the Australian Stock Exchange.
The healthcare and biotechnology index, to be launched on September 1, is expected to provide a focus for domestic and international interest in the sector, and may help boost turnover, analysts say.
"It draws attention to the fact that such stocks are around, when they have been previously hidden away in miscellaneous industrials and services," said a Sydney-based analyst.
The index will contain 11 companies with a combined market capitalisation of about A$4.9 billion.

They range in size from pharmaceutical manufacturers CSL Ltd and F.H.Faulding and Co Ltd, each with a market capitalisation of around A$1 billion, to biotechnology group Progen Industries Ltd, capitalised at about A$108 million.

Ramsay Healthcare Ltd, which announced its float plans this month is another likely candidate, but transport, security and healthcare giant Mayne Nickless Ltd has been omitted, at least for the present.

Cortecs International Ltd, which has 80 percent of its shareholding offshore, is changing its main listing to London in order to participate in the exchange's new automated trading system but will be part of the new index.
Much of the interest in Australian biotechnology stocks comes at present from the retail end of the market, although CSL, Faulding and Cortecs have attracted offshore support, analysts said.
In the smaller stocks, institutional interest has often been dampened by lack of liqudity, the amount of volatility and a lack of expertise in valuation.
"There's a lot of volatility involved in some of them because of the nature of the companies," said Macquarie Equities analyst Simon Jones.
"A lot of the value is derived from trial results in the same way resource stocks are driven by exploration results."

The inclusion in the sector of more stable private hospital operators, such as Ramsay and Australian Hospital Care Ltd, could boost local interest, while the index itself may promote overseas interest.
"The international factor is quite important," said Intersuisse research director Howard Elton.
"There is a lot of interest in our pharmaceutical stocks by overseas investors, and when America is hot on pharmaceuticals that will flow through to ours," he said.
One Sydney-based firm, which keeps a broad 33-stock health care index, said turnover is generally 0.6-0.7 times turnover in the All Ordinaries index, adjusting for market capitalisation.
Its index has outperformed the All Industrials over the past five years, but during the past three months has underperformed the strong run in the wider market.
Faulding and Cortecs have disappointed in recent months, although Cortecs has rallied recently on plans to register an anti-bone wasting drug.
Strong performers include pharmaceutical researcher Amrad, hearing implant group Cochlear Ltd and protective equipment and eyewear maker OPSM Protector Ltd.

-- The health care and biotechnology sector index consists of companies involved in industries ranging from pharmaceutical, biotechnology, hospital management, health/medical services, and therapeutic products and services.
They are (with market capitalisation included):
Amrad Corp Ltd (A$275 million),
Australian Hospital Care Ltd (A$258 million),
Australian Pharmaceutical Industries Ltd (A$332 million),
Biota Holdings Ltd (A$300 million),
Cochlear Ltd (A$230 million),
Cortecs International Ltd (A$736 million),
CSL Ltd (A$1.00 billion),
F.H. Faulding and Co Ltd (A$962 million),
OPSM Protector Ltd (A$508 million),
Sonic Healthcare Ltd (A$204 million), and
Progen Industries Ltd (A$108 million).
